181.quote_or_event: “It is not good to slander anyone, but the foolish, self-willed manmukhs still do it.”
181.explanation: Guru Amar Das teaches that slandering anyone at all is never good, and that it is the self-willed manmukh who falls into the habit.
181.tie_back: The Kural says that even a man with no other virtue earns some credit if he does not backbite; Guru Amar Das likewise singles out slander as a wrong to be avoided toward anyone.
181.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 755, Raag Soohee, Guru Amar Das (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
181._accuracy_note: Reasonable but partial: both condemn slander outright, but the verse lacks the Kural's provocative concession that a non-slanderer is good even if he does nothing else right.

182.quote_or_event: “Those who have one thing in their heart, and something else in their mouth, are judged to be false.”
182.explanation: In a hymn preserved in the Guru Granth Sahib, Sheikh Farid says that those whose words do not match their hearts are counted false.
182.tie_back: The Kural judges the man who tears others down behind their backs and then smiles falsely to their faces as worse than an open evildoer; Farid names that same split between heart and mouth as falseness.
182.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 488, Raag Aasaa, Sheikh Farid (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
182._accuracy_note: Reasonable fit on two-faced falseness; Farid's verse is about sincere love of God rather than backbiting, and it does not rank the vice against open wrongdoing.

183.quote_or_event: “O Nanak, no one else is truly alive; those who merely live shall depart in dishonor”
183.explanation: In a salok of Vaar Maajh, Guru Nanak teaches that only one whose mind holds the Lord is truly alive, and that a life which loses honour is not worth having.
183.tie_back: The Kural says it is better to die than to stay alive by backbiting and falsehood; Guru Nanak likewise rates a dishonoured life as no true life at all.
183.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 142, Raag Maajh (Vaar Maajh, salok), Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
183._accuracy_note: Reasonable but partial: both rank honour above mere survival, but Guru Nanak locates true life in remembrance of God, not specifically in refraining from slander.

184.quote_or_event: “Do not utter even a single harsh word; your True Lord and Master abides in all.”
184.explanation: In a salok preserved in the Guru Granth Sahib, Sheikh Farid forbids even one harsh word to anyone, since the Lord dwells in every person.
184.tie_back: The Kural allows even harsh words spoken to a person's face, so long as one never speaks thoughtlessly behind his back; Farid's verse shares the concern for careful speech but goes further, forbidding harshness altogether.
184.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1384, Salok Sheikh Farid (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
184._accuracy_note: Next-best only, with a real tension: the Kural tolerates harsh words to the face, while this verse rejects all harsh speech, and it does not address speaking behind someone's back.

185.quote_or_event: “We are good at talking, but our actions are bad. Mentally, we are impure and black, but outwardly, we appear white.”
185.explanation: In a salok of Sri Raag ki Vaar, Guru Nanak confesses the human gap between fine words and bad conduct, and between a dark inner mind and a clean outward show.
185.tie_back: The Kural says that however much a man talks of virtue, his backbiting shows his heart is not given to it; Guru Nanak exposes that same gap between virtuous talk and the inner heart.
185.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 85, Sri Raag (Sri Raag ki Vaar, salok), Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
185._accuracy_note: Strong thematic fit on talk of virtue hiding an impure heart; the verse does not name backbiting as the evidence that gives the speaker away.

186.quote_or_event: “Fareed, if you have a keen understanding, then do not write black marks against anyone else. Look underneath your own collar instead.”
186.explanation: Sheikh Farid tells the discerning person to stop recording other people's faults and to look honestly at his own.
186.tie_back: The Kural warns that one who spreads others' faults will have his own worst faults picked out and told; Farid turns the same scrutiny back on oneself before others do it.
186.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1378, Salok Sheikh Farid, Salok 6 (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
186._accuracy_note: Reasonable but partial: both link exposing others' faults to one's own faults, but Farid counsels self-examination rather than warning of retaliation.

187.quote_or_event: “O Nanak, speaking insipid words, the body and mind become insipid.”
187.explanation: In Asa di Vaar Guru Nanak teaches that harsh, graceless speech dries up the speaker himself, body and mind.
187.tie_back: The Kural says those who cannot win friends with pleasant talk fall into divisive speech that drives off even their own; Guru Nanak likewise warns that harsh speech leaves the speaker sour and estranged.
187.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 473, Raag Aasaa (Asa di Vaar, salok), Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
187._accuracy_note: Next-best: the verse condemns harsh speech and praises sweet speech, but does not describe the Kural's specific harm of splitting friends and kin.

188.quote_or_event: “He slanders others, and pollutes himself with his own filth.”
188.explanation: Guru Amar Das teaches that the habit of slandering others dirties the slanderer's own mind.
188.tie_back: The Kural asks what a person who habitually broadcasts even his intimates' faults will not do to strangers; Guru Amar Das shows how deeply such a habit corrupts the one who has it.
188.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 88, Sri Raag (Sri Raag ki Vaar, salok), Guru Amar Das (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
188._accuracy_note: Next-best only: it condemns habitual slander, but lacks the Kural's a fortiori argument from slandering close friends to slandering strangers.

189.quote_or_event: “The mythical bull is Dharma, the son of compassion; this is what patiently holds the earth in its place.”
189.explanation: In Japji Guru Nanak reinterprets the myth of the bull that carries the earth: what really holds the world up is dharma, born of compassion.
189.tie_back: The Kural wonders whether the earth bears the weight of the backbiter only out of regard for dharma; Japji says it is dharma itself that patiently holds the earth up.
189.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 3, Japji Sahib, Pauri 16, Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
189._accuracy_note: Reasonable but partial: the image of dharma patiently bearing the earth matches strikingly, but Japji says nothing about slanderers, so the Kural's irony is not present.

190.quote_or_event: “Kabeer, I am the worst of all. Everyone else is good.”
190.explanation: Bhagat Kabir, whose saloks are part of the Guru Granth Sahib, models a humility that looks first at one's own faults and sees others as good.
190.tie_back: The Kural asks whether any harm could come to living beings if people saw their own faults as clearly as others'; Kabir turns that clear sight wholly on himself.
190.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1364, Salok Bhagat Kabir (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
190._accuracy_note: Strong fit on turning fault-finding inward; the Kural's claim that this would end harm to all beings is implied rather than stated, and Kabir is a bhagat whose hymns are Sikh scripture, not a Guru.
